messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Marcus

Marcus was fifty-two when he first came to the clinic, though he moved with the careful deliberation of someone much older. A professional musician—he played classical guitar and had once performed at regional venues across California—he arrived for his intake appointment twenty minutes early, having circled the building twice to assess exits and sightlines. The stalking had begun three years ago, though its origins remained partly obscured to him even now. A woman he'd briefly dated, someone he'd met through a mutual friend at a concert, had become fixated on him. What had started as persistent texts and emails escalated into her showing up at venues where he performed, waiting outside his apartment, calling him at hours when she knew he'd be home. The police had issued a restraining order eighteen months in, but by then the damage to Marcus's sense of safety had already calcified.

He could not reconstruct the timeline of those early months with any clarity. There were gaps in what he remembered—entire weeks when she'd followed him to different neighborhoods, to coffee shops, to his ex-wife's house, and Marcus could only piece together these episodes from her own messages, from police reports, from the concerned calls of friends. The fragmentation terrified him because it meant she had been present in his life in ways he couldn't fully account for, couldn't fully remember. What haunted him most were the sudden, unbidden fragments that would surface without warning: the sound of her voice outside his door at three in the morning, the specific shade of her car in a parking lot, the feeling of being watched from across a crowded venue. These pieces would arrive with complete sensory force—he could smell the perfume she wore, could hear the exact cadence of her breathing—and then vanish as quickly as they'd come, leaving him disoriented and questioning what was real.

Marcus had come to believe he was weak, that a stronger man would have seen the danger earlier, would have handled it differently, would have been able to protect himself without needing police intervention. This conviction—that he was fundamentally inadequate—fed directly into his hypervigilance. He watched other people constantly now, scanning faces for signs of threat, interpreting neutral expressions as harbingers of malice. In his mind, if he had been stronger, more perceptive, less naive, he would not need to be this exhausted sentinel. The institutional failure compounded this self-judgment; the restraining order had felt like a bureaucratic gesture, a piece of paper that had not actually stopped her from finding him. The police had been sympathetic but ultimately powerless. The courts had failed him. This conviction that the systems meant to protect him were hollow made him feel more alone, more convinced that his own weakness was the only honest assessment of reality.

The memory gaps and those sudden sensory intrusions had become entangled with his threat assessment in ways that made him feel trapped. Because he couldn't remember when she'd been watching him, because fragments would arrive unbidden and vivid, he could never be certain when the danger had truly passed. Every unfamiliar place became a potential ambush; he avoided new restaurants, new routes to venues, anywhere he couldn't quickly map exits and sight lines. At night, the vigilance intensified. He felt safer during daylight, when he could see clearly and assess threats visually, but darkness made him feel hunted. He'd stopped accepting evening performance bookings. His income had declined. His ex-wife, concerned but ultimately exhausted by his withdrawal, had stopped calling as frequently.

The fragments still came—a flash of that specific perfume in a grocery store, a car that matched the color of hers turning a corner—and each one sent him spiraling back into the conviction that he was being watched, that his weakness had made him vulnerable, that no one could truly help him. He had come to the clinic because his last remaining regular gig, a Sunday morning teaching position at a community center, had become unsustainable; his hypervigilance was affecting his ability to teach, to trust even his students. What he most feared was that the vigilance was permanent, that he would never feel safe again, that the weakness he'd discovered in himself was not something that had been exposed by the stalking but something that defined him entirely.
